data.coverage_note: NASA's reconstruction covers the whole trip without gaps.

sunlight_h.no_margin_reason: Only the Moon's shadow is involved, cast by a smooth sphere: lunar mountains move its edges by seconds, which is not worked out here.

heard_h.no_margin_reason: Station masks are published without a tolerance.

longest_shadow_h.no_margin_reason: Only the Moon's shadow is involved, cast by a smooth sphere: lunar mountains move its edges by seconds, which is not worked out here.

longest_unheard_h.no_margin_reason: Its edges are set by station masks.

data.burns_note: Found where NASA's reconstruction leaves the force model by more than 0.05 m/s in half an hour, up to the arrival at the Moon; each is shown as one instant. A burn in a gap of the reconstruction is not seen. Burns in lunar orbit are not listed: there the force model and the reconstruction part by about 1 m/s at each close pass of the Moon, as much as a small burn. From 2024-01-08 to 2024-01-18 the reconstruction shows a steady push, not separate burns.
data.corrections_note: It did not reach the Moon, so there is no arrival to budget for.

belt_hours.source: Inside the belts: where the maps hold electrons above 1 MeV or protons above 10 MeV. AE8/AP8 MAX (IRBEM, with 0.3 degrees/year longitudinal South Atlantic Anomaly drift compensation): the year before averaged 125 sunspots a day, against 2 to 126 over the 11 years before (OMNI), so the solar-maximum maps.

electron_fluence_gt1mev.source: AE8/AP8 MAX (IRBEM, with 0.3 degrees/year longitudinal South Atlantic Anomaly drift compensation): the year before averaged 125 sunspots a day, against 2 to 126 over the 11 years before (OMNI), so the solar-maximum maps. The solar-minimum maps give 1.6e+10.

fluence_gt10mev.source: Trapped protons above 10 MeV. AE8/AP8 MAX (IRBEM, with 0.3 degrees/year longitudinal South Atlantic Anomaly drift compensation): the year before averaged 125 sunspots a day, against 2 to 126 over the 11 years before (OMNI), so the solar-maximum maps. The solar-minimum maps give 2.8e+08.

gcr_dose_mgy_day.source: From 18.9 cGy a year in silicon, measured by CRaTER's microdosimeter on LRO on 20 June 2009, about 10,000 km from the Moon (Mazur et al. 2011, as given by Schwadron et al. 2012, JGR 117, E00H13), scaled by the cosmic-ray model's change between then (W = 5) and 2024-01 (W = 90): ×0.41 (Matthiä et al. 2013, W from the Oulu neutron monitor, NMDB). ±30 % covers the scaling.

radiation.surface_note: It was lost before reaching the Moon, so there is no surface dose.
radiation.sep_note: No solar particle event crossed NOAA's threshold (10 pfu above 10 MeV at GOES) during the trip (NASA DONKI).

fluence_gt10mev.no_margin_reason: As measured at 1 AU outside Earth's magnetic field (taken as arriving evenly from all directions); GOES proton detector, 5-minute averages (NOAA NCEI), 1989-10-19 12:00 to 1989-11-01 00:00 UTC; peak 42,200 pfu above 10 MeV (NOAA's list: 40,000).

As measured at 1 AU outside Earth's magnetic field (taken as arriving evenly from all directions); GOES proton detector, 5-minute averages (NOAA NCEI), 2003-10-28 11:00 to 2003-11-01 00:00 UTC; peak 29,500 pfu above 10 MeV (NOAA's list: 29,500).

As measured at 1 AU outside Earth's magnetic field (taken as arriving evenly from all directions); King (1974), J. Spacecraft Rockets 11, 401: fitted spectrum J(>E) = 7.9e9 exp((30 - E)/26.5) per cm², as SPENVIS gives it.

radiation.screening_note: Screening only: long-term average belt maps (good to about a factor of two), cosmic-ray dose scaled from measurements (±30 %), and past events as they were measured at 1 AU. None of it accounts for the spacecraft's own shielding. Confirm in SPENVIS, OLTARIS or CREME-MC before any design decision.

parts.note: A screening estimate: belt maps good to about a factor of two, cosmic-ray dose ±30 %; confirm in SPENVIS, OLTARIS or CREME-MC.
NASA's reconstruction as archived; its own accuracy is not published with it.
Spherical Earth and Moon; the ± on sunlight and the longest shadow is the change when Earth's shadow is made 2 % larger for its atmosphere.
A station 'can see' the spacecraft when it is above the station's mask; antenna pointing and bookings are not modelled.
